title: Design a Content Moderation Pipeline
summary: An async, multi-stage pipeline that screens user content before and after it goes live — the pipeline shape and feedback loop are the hard part, not the classifier itself.

slides.markdown:
Design a system that screens every post, comment, and image for policy violations, at platform scale — think the pipeline behind a report button and the automated filters that catch most violations before anyone reports them at all.

Think of it like airport security: a fast automated scan handles the overwhelming majority of bags, and only a small, genuinely ambiguous slice gets pulled aside for a human to look at closely. The classifier itself (what counts as a violation) is a model-training problem; this topic is about the conveyor belt around it — how content moves through automated and human review without either becoming the bottleneck.

**Functional:** screen submitted content automatically, route ambiguous cases to human reviewers, act on confirmed violations (remove, warn, ban), and let users appeal a takedown decision.

**Non-functional:** decide **pre-publish vs post-publish** screening per content type — pre-publish blocks a violation from ever going live but adds latency to every single post; post-publish lets content go live instantly but risks brief exposure before removal. **Latency budget** differs sharply by stage: the automated pass needs to run in milliseconds, human review can take hours. **Appeal flow** must exist, since automated and even human decisions are sometimes wrong.

slides.sectionTitle: Back-of-envelope: content volume vs reviewer capacity
slides.markdown:
A platform with 500M daily active users posting an average of 2 pieces of content/day produces 1B items/day (~11,500/sec) needing at least an automated pass. If an automated classifier flags 2% as borderline, that's 20M items/day needing human review.

A human reviewer might handle roughly 500-1,000 review decisions per shift; at 20M/day, that implies tens of thousands of reviewer-shifts daily — clearly impossible to staff for the full flagged volume without further prioritization. The numbers force the real design question: given a review queue that will always exceed human capacity, what gets looked at first?

`submitForReview(content)` is called automatically on every piece of published content, not just user-reported ones — it's the entry point into the automated classifier pass. `reportContent(id, reason)` lets any user flag existing content, injecting it into the same review pipeline out of band. `reviewDecision(id, verdict)` is the human reviewer's action, recording an outcome (approve, remove, escalate) that then triggers downstream enforcement.

Treating both automated submission and user reports as the same `submitForReview` entry point (rather than two separate pipelines) keeps prioritization, dedup, and enforcement logic in one place instead of two.

slides.sectionTitle: Pipeline design: automated pass, then human review for borderline cases
slides.markdown:
Content flows through two stages. The **automated classifier pass** runs on every item, in milliseconds, and outputs a confidence score plus category (spam, harassment, graphic content, and so on). High-confidence violations are auto-removed; high-confidence clean content passes through untouched; everything in between — the genuinely ambiguous middle — is queued for human review.

This three-way split (clearly bad, clearly fine, unclear) is what keeps the pipeline sustainable: it's designed explicitly so human reviewers only ever see the sliver of content a machine couldn't confidently classify, not the full firehose.

![Content ingest through the automated classifier's three-way split, a priority queue, human review, and final action](assets/content-flow.svg)

The priority queue sitting between the classifier and the human reviewer is doing real work, not just buffering — it's what decides which of the millions of daily borderline items a limited reviewer pool actually gets to before the next batch arrives.

assets.alt: Content ingest through the automated classifier's three-way split, a priority queue, human review, and final action

slides.markdown:
First-come-first-served is the wrong default for a queue that will never be fully drained: a low-visibility post sitting unreviewed for a day causes little harm, while a rapidly-reshared post heading toward virality causes far more if a genuine violation stays up even a few extra hours.

A better priority signal blends the classifier's confidence (how likely this is a real violation) with a **virality/reach estimate** (how fast it's currently spreading) — items that are both plausibly violating and rapidly spreading jump to the front, even if they arrived in the queue after items that are neither.

| | Block-before-publish | Publish-then-remove |
|---|---|---|
| Latency added to every post | Real — every post waits on at least the automated pass | Minimal — publish is immediate, screening happens after |
| Risk if screening is wrong | False positives block legitimate content before anyone sees it | Violations are briefly visible before takedown |
| Best suited to | High-stakes categories (e.g. child safety), where any exposure is unacceptable | Most general content, where brief exposure is an acceptable cost for instant publishing |
| Typical implementation | Synchronous automated check in the publish path | Async screening, `publish()` returns immediately |

**How to decide:** default to publish-then-remove for the bulk of content, since the latency cost of gating everyone applies constantly while violations are comparatively rare — reserve block-before-publish for categories where even brief exposure is unacceptable.

slides.sectionTitle: Feedback loop: reviewer decisions retraining the filters
slides.markdown:
Every human reviewer decision is a labeled data point the automated classifier didn't confidently have on its own — that's exactly why the item reached a human in the first place. Feeding these decisions back as training data lets the classifier's confidence on similar future content improve over time, gradually shrinking the slice that needs human review.

Without this loop, the classifier stays frozen at its original accuracy while the volume of borderline content grows with the platform — the review queue only gets worse, never better. This is the mechanism that keeps a fixed-size human reviewer pool viable as the platform scales.

![A takedown dispute enters a separate appeal queue, gets a different reviewer, and both outcomes log back into the feedback loop](assets/appeal-flow.svg)

Routing appeals to a different reviewer than the original decision is deliberate — it avoids a reviewer simply re-confirming their own earlier judgment, and both outcomes (uphold or restore) still feed the same training loop as an ordinary review decision.

assets.alt: A takedown dispute enters a separate appeal queue, gets a different reviewer, and both outcomes log back into the feedback loop

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a synchronous moderation check on the publish path
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Run the full moderation check synchronously before confirming a post — it's safer to screen everything up front."

**Why it's wrong:** even a fast automated classifier adds real, cumulative latency to every single publish call, for the vast majority of content that will turn out to be entirely fine — and if the classifier ever depends on a slower downstream service, that latency compounds directly into the user-facing publish experience for everyone, all the time.

**Correct model:** publish content immediately for most categories, screen asynchronously in the background, and reserve synchronous, block-before-publish checks for the narrow set of high-stakes categories where any exposure is genuinely unacceptable — don't pay the latency tax platform-wide for a risk that's concentrated in a small slice of content.
